pages.description: Under a tax treaty, foreign country residents receive a reduced tax rate or an exemption from U.S. income tax on certain income they receive from U.S. sources.
pages.text: Tax treaties | Internal Revenue Service Skip to main content Tax treaties More In File Individuals Businesses and self-employed Charities and nonprofits International taxpayers Individuals - international Businesses - international Foreign Account Tax Compliance Act (FATCA) Governmental liaisons Federal, state and local governments Indian tribal governments Tax exempt bonds Taxpayer identification numbers (TIN) Overview The United States has income tax treaties with a number of foreign countries. Under these treaties, residents (not necessarily citizens) of foreign countries may be eligible to be taxed at a reduced rate or exempt from U.S. income taxes on certain items of income they receive from sources within the United States. These reduced rates and exemptions vary among countries and specific items of income. If the treaty does not cover a particular kind of income, or if there is no treaty between your country and the United States, you must pay tax on the income in the same way and at the same rates shown in the instructions for Form 1040-NR, U.S. Nonresident Alien Income Tax Return . Also see Publication 519, U.S. Tax Guide for Aliens , and Publication 515, Withholding of Tax on Nonresident Aliens and Foreign Entities . Many of the individual states of the United States tax the income of their residents. Some states honor the provisions of U.S. tax treaties and some states do not. We continue to move toward issue-based examinations and a compliance program that focuses on high-risk issues using one or multiple treatment streams. A treatment stream is a single or a combination of compliance actions we will implement to achieve an initiative’s goal. The idea is to respond with the right treatment stream to maintain high compliance across the TE/GE filing population. This approach makes efficient use of IRS knowledge and deploys the right resources to address noncompliance issues. Our compliance program involves a thorough analysis of data to support the identification and evaluation of a compliance issue, a deliberate consideration of potential treatment streams, decisions about the resources to be deployed, identification of training, and tools needed, as well as a robust feedback mechanism to ensure all elements of an initiative are continuously improved. Technology Commercialization Fund The Technology Commercialization Fund (TCF) is a U.S. Department of Energy program that helps move innovations developed at DOE National Laboratories, plants, and sites into the marketplace. Established by Congress in the Energy Policy Act of 2005, TCF invests millions of dollars each year to bridge the gap between research and commercial application. The program supports partnerships between DOE facilities and industry, universities, and other organizations to advance technologies with strong market potential. The team managed to electronically tag 10 of them and the largest was 60cm (23ins) in length and weighted 435g (0.9lbs). Ward said: "European eels start to migrate downstream during autumn and winter, when river discharges increase. Get our Newsletter! Like many birds, domestic turkeys, including this group at the Smithsonian's National Zoo in Washington, D.C., are social animals. Smithsonian/Brett Kuxhausen 1. Humans have been raising turkeys for thousands of years. Although indigenous peoples in North America have hunted wild turkeys since the end of the last Ice Age, the animals were first domesticated in Mexico around 2,000 years ago. Dinner wasn’t the original goal: archaeological evidence suggests turkeys were initially kept so their feathers could be used in clothing and ceremonial regalia. By A.D. 500, people were raising turkeys in what is now the United States too, judging by archaeological remains from caves in Arizona and New Mexico. Even so, those weren’t the birds that English settlers ate in the Thirteen Colonies. The domestic turkey descends from a southern Mexican bird that the Spanish took home in the 1500s. The birds then spread through Europe, and colonists brought them back across the Atlantic. The bird’s English name may reflect this long-distance trade: turkeys are thought to have reached England along winding trading routes that first passed through the country of Turkey. 2. pages.text: Tens of thousands of tents flooded after heavy rains in Gaza Skip to content Site search Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Weather Newsletters Tens of thousands of tents flooded after heavy rains in Gaza 7 November 2026 Share Save Add as preferred on Google Emer Moreau Getty Images Ninety percent of Gaza residents have been displaced by the Israeli war against Hamas Heavy rains have flooded tens of thousands of tents where displaced residents have been living in Gaza, with a United Nations official saying almost everyone in the territory needs help. Residents used pots and pans to clear water from their flooded tents, with some saying they were left without shelter. Jonathan Veitch, the Unicef representative for Palestine, said the "desperate" situation was being made worse by Israeli restrictions on the entry of heavy machinery and supplies such as engine oil. Some 90% of Gaza residents have been displaced by the Israeli war against Hamas, many of them multiple times, with limited access to clean water and sanitation. Aid agencies say the situation is likely to worsen with the start of the rainy season. Tetanus: Causes and How It Spreads For Everyone Sept. 10, 2026 Español Key points Tetanus spores from the environment enter the body through cuts or wounds. Tetanus doesn't spread from person to person. It is possible to have tetanus infection more than once. Prevent tetanus by staying up to date with vaccinations and seeking appropriate care after a wound. Causes Bacteria live in the environment Spores of Clostridium tetani are common in the environment, including soil, dust, and manure. The spores develop into bacteria when they enter the body. Common exposures The spores can get into someone's body through broken skin, usually through injuries. Tetanus bacteria are more likely to infect certain breaks in the skin, including: Wounds contaminated with dirt, feces (poop), or saliva (spit) Puncture wounds (wounds caused by an object, like a nail or needle) Injuries with dead tissue (e.g., burns, crush injuries, frostbite) Dead tissue is a concern because it can promote bacteria growth. pages.description: Scientists call the events permafrost detachment slides. Instead of thawing from the top down, these landslides seem to originate from a weakened base
pages.text: Thawing Permafrost May Have Created a New Type of Landslide, Which Could Become More Common as the World Warms Skip to main content A scar left by the 2018 Redstone River permafrost landslide, one of the two events investigated in the new study. Adapted from J. M. Young et al., Geophysical Research Letters , 2026 In 2017 and 2018, a pair of strange landslides moved huge masses of rock and dirt in Canada’s Northwest Territories. The events occurred in the central Mackenzie Valley, and one of them even dammed a river and created a lake . The two natural disasters are part of a new class of landslides scientists are calling “permafrost detachment slides” in a study published in the journal Geophysical Research Letters in September. They may have been partially triggered by severe wildfires that occurred in 1995, which destabilized the ground and allowed the base of the permafrost to thaw. What’s more, these events may become more common as the planet continues to warm. “It’s a very dramatic manifestation of the changing climate,” says study co-author Joseph Young , a geoscientist who conducted the work at the University of Alberta in Canada, to Matt Simon at Grist . “They’ve only started happening in the last 10, 15 years, and it’s a very drastic and abrupt change in the landscape.” Young and his colleagues began the study after seeing something strange in the Northwest Territories in 2019. While conducting field research, they spotted large landslide scars in valleys that they knew were stable permafrost , or permanently frozen earth, reports Stephanie Pappas for Live Science

By Nicholas St. Fleur Published March 30, 2026 A newly discovered Spinosaurus sporting a bizarre, curved blade-like crest has snatched the headlines. But this massive carnivore is far from the only odd-looking prehistoric predator out there. In this episode of Dead World, our archaeology and paleontology video series, we look at some bizarre raptor-like dinosaurs that menaced the Mesozoic. These dinosaurs show just how strange evolution can get. Xenovenator , a recently discovered troodontid from Mexico, had a thickened skull that it may have used as a battering ram. Knowable Magazine Whether it’s gushing from a bumped nose or pooling atop a pricked finger, our blood is some hue of red. But red-bloodedness isn’t universal in the animal kingdom. In some creatures, the vital fluid is purple; in others it’s yellow, green or even white. What imparts these different colors to the liquid of life? To find out, Knowable magazine waded into the research and spoke with a couple of scientists who have studied the stuff. Here’s what’s known about the science behind the hues. Bizarre blues and purples The rich red of vertebrate blood comes from hemoglobin, a protein in red blood cells that contains iron atoms. Hemoglobin’s job is to deliver oxygen—and its iron atoms, which grab onto oxygen, make our blood look red. pages.text: The Complicated Social Life of a Tyrannosaurus Rex | National Geographic SCIENCE Why Everything We Thought We Knew About T. Rex is Getting … Messier Fossil evidence has shifted our view of T. rex from a complete loner tyrant into a more nuanced carnivore. Scarred skulls, scraped ground, and fossilized trackways suggest adult tyrannosaurs lived largely solitary lives, like modern big cats, but also gathered in communal display arenas to woo potential mates. GERD LUDWIG, National Geographic Image Collection By Riley Black Published October 8, 2026 Every time I’m in New York, I have to visit her. She’s always waiting in the same place, standing on the fourth floor of the American Museum of Natural History, grinning so wide that her teeth gleam under the bright lights. Experts know her as AMNH 5027. I know her as the first T yrannosaurus rex I ever met. Before the discovery of “Sue,” “Stan,” “Scotty,” and many other famous skeletons of Earth’s last great carnivorous dinosaur, AMNH 5027 was the icon. The partial skeleton was the first T . rex to include a complete skull – only slightly smushed. It left no doubt that the dinosaur was an impressive flesh-ripper, reconstructed with jaws agape when the museum’s paleontologists assembled real bones and casts in the world’s first great introduction to the dinosaur. (And, when Michael Crichton’s Jurassic Park needed a skeletal dinosaur for the cover, AMNH 5027 was the model.) But to paleontologists, the oasis is sacred because of something far older and far more legendary: Spinosaurus . The first ever specimen of this ferocious river monster was collected here more than a hundred years ago, along with fossils of several other enigmatic dinosaurs. SCIENCE LAELAPS The Echoes of Toothed Birds By Riley Black Published May 22, 2015 • 4 min read Whenever I spot a grebe, I try to imagine the bird with teeth. This is another symptom of a chronically fossiliferous mind. You see, these snake-necked swimming birds have traditionally been taken as a proxy for a specific sort of ancient avian called hesperornithiforms. Best known by, as you might guess, Hesperornis – these toothed birds pioneered the diving lifestyle between 113 and 66 million years ago. Today’s grebes and loons look like edentulous echos of these lost Cretaceous days, or, as beautifully expressed by ornithologist William Beebe : When in the depth of the winter, a full hundred miles from the nearest land, one sees a loon in the path of the steamer, listens to its weird, maniacal laughter, and sees it slowly sink downward through the green waters, it truly seems a hint of the bird-life of long-past ages. No surprise, then, that paleontologists past sometimes considered loons and grebes to be the descendants of Hesperornis . Their bones carry the same superficial similarity. But this is an evolutionary ruse known as convergence. Loons and grebes are copycats that independently took up the same lifestyle as the toothed birds that dove after fish in warm Cretaceous seas and sometimes wound up in the stomachs of monstrous marine reptiles. Diamantas, J.D., Acting Commissioner of Food and Drugs Kyle A. Diamantas, J.D. There may be no better illustration of the critical and integral role the U.S. Food and Drug Administration has played in the history of our nation’s health than the timely juxtaposition of two anniversaries occurring this year – our nation’s 250th and the FDA’s 120th. Steps include the president creating the budget plan and Congress’s work creating funding bills for the president to sign. Annual funding areas Every year, the U.S. Congress begins work on a federal budget for the next fiscal year. The federal government’s fiscal year runs from October 1 of one calendar year through September 30 of the next. And the annual budget covers three spending areas: Mandatory spending - funding for Social Security, Medicare, veterans benefits, and other spending required by law. This typically uses over half of all funding. Discretionary spending - federal agency funding. Congress sets funding levels for these each year. This usually accounts for around a third of all funding. Interest on the debt - this usually uses less than 10 percent of all funding. Creating the U.S. federal budget The budget planning begins a year before the budget is to go into effect. Federal agencies create budget requests and submit them to the White House Office of Management and Budget (OMB). OMB refers to the agencies’ requests as it develops the budget proposal for the president. The president submits the budget proposal to Congress early the next year. Francois Gohier/Universal Images Group via Getty Images Nearly 1,000 feet below the sea off the coast of Norway’s Svalbard archipelago, on a glass cable the width of a human hair, scientists detect a massive object moving through the water. It’s so big that the water it displaces when it moves produces low-frequency waves that radiate outward from its body. These waves ripple away toward the seafloor, where they stretch the tiny glass cable, buried beneath the seabed, almost imperceptibly. Onshore, laser pulses are fired down the cable, and as the light travels, microscopic imperfections scatter the light in the glass. SCIENCE LAELAPS The Jurassic Shield By Riley Black Published June 26, 2015 • 7 min read Some dinosaurs are better at hiding than others. There’s no single reason for their edge. Some were rare. Others too small to gain much notice from the paleontologists who were set on finding large, imposing specimens for museum centerpieces. Still more became preserved in slices of rock that haven’t gained the attention of the most famed quarries. Whatever the reasons, though, a big, heavily-armored dinosaur was able to escape the notice of paleontologists despite over a century of Jurassic exploration. North America’s Morrison Formation is a fossiliferous wonderland. Spectacular bonebeds dot its reach from Canada to Mexico, and it was one of the focal points for the great Bone Wars between O.C. Marsh and E.D. Cope in the late 19th century. Apatosaurus , Allosaurus , Camarasaurus , Diplodocus and more were the products of that feud. Strangest of all was Stegosaurus – a 30-foot-long quadruped with a tiny head, flashy plates along its back, and a set of four spikes jutting from the tip of its tail. Marsh named the bizarre animal in 1877, and ever since Stegosaurus has held the banner for the plated, spiky armored dinosaurs that were eventually replaced by ankylosaurs. Yann Garin By Lauren Paige Richeson Published October 15, 2026 Long before our messages arrived with a buzz, a letter could introduce itself by touch. Without even glimpsing the handwriting inside, the paper itself announced a family name, a profession, a crest, or a ceremony—not merely a decoration, but a declaration. In Paris, one of the most refined ways to create that impression was with timbrage au balancier , or pendulum stamping. Developed in the 19th-century world of engraving and correspondence, the technique gave calling cards, invitations, letterheads, and envelope flaps something ordinary ink could not provide: a feeling. Everything from a coat of arms to a pair of initials could rise from the page in dense color and varying depths. But as correspondence slipped from paper to pixels and luxury printing pressed faster towards mechanized processes, the manual craft began to lose the world that sustained it. From roughly the 16th to 19th centuries, much of the Earth was gripped by a persistent frigid cold. It left ripples through history—and some lessons for today’s climate crisis. By Kieran Mulvaney Published February 20, 2024 Thousands of people walking and playing across the frozen River Thames. Soldiers on horseback capturing ships stuck in the ice. Indigenous populations using snowshoes to outfox English interlopers. Accused witches put on trial as their communities struggled to explain crop failures and extreme cold. These were some of the images that define the Little Ice Age—a period of several centuries last millennium in which parts of the Northern Hemisphere grappled with a persistent cold. But what caused the Little Ice Age, how long did it last, how did people adapt to its frigid grip—and what lessons can we learn as we enter our own period of climatic change? ( Broken Baculum a Sign of Painful Ice Age Injury) What is the Little Ice Age—and what caused it? The Little Ice Age was not a true ice age—average cooling was probably only in the order of 0.5 degrees Celsius , or 1 degree Fahrenheit—nor was it consistently cold.

pages.description: The National Geologic Map Database (NGMDB) is a distributed archive of geoscience information for the Nation. We welcome you to explore the archive, view the maps, and help us to improve this resource.

pages.title: The National Portrait Gallery Wasn't Allowed to Acquire Photographs When It Opened in 1968. Fifty Years Later, the Smithsonian Museum's Collection Has Grown to 11,000 Photos and Counting
pages.description: A new exhibition at the Washington, D.C. gallery celebrates half a century of collecting through portraits spanning the history of photography. Featured figures include President Abraham Lincoln, journalist Ida B. Wells and inventor Thomas Edison

Featured figures include President Abraham Lincoln, journalist Ida B. Wells and inventor Thomas Edison A 1963 gelatin silver print of Malcolm X by Gordon Parks National Portrait Gallery, Smithsonian Institution / © Gordon Parks A 1963 gelatin silver print of Malcolm X by Gordon Parks National Portrait Gallery, Smithsonian Institution / © Gordon Parks When the Smithsonian’s National Portrait Gallery opened to the public in 1968, its curators had a clear remit : to collect “painted or sculptured likenesses” of individuals who had left their mark on American history and culture. Photography didn’t make the cut, despite the fact that the medium had been invented nearly a century and a half earlier. This restriction wasn’t instated for aesthetic or ideological reasons. Instead, it came down to a turf war in the nation’s capital.
